subject: Biology

stem: A monitoring program recorded annual vessel traffic and the percentage of stranded turtles with vessel-strike injuries (VSI).

parts.label: a
parts.html: Identify the year with the highest VSI percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Describe the relationship between vessel traffic and VSI.

parts.label: c
parts.html: State two limitations of using stranded turtles to estimate population injury rate.

parts.label: d
parts.html: Calculate the percentage increase in annual vessel traffic from 2012 to 2020.

parts.label: e
parts.html: Suggest why species may differ in strike risk.

parts.label: f
parts.html: Evaluate the conclusion that vessel traffic causes VSI.

questions.title: Sea-turtle strandings and vessel traffic

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Overall positive association; VSI rises from 12% to 33% as traffic rises; 2016 is lower than expected and 2020 is highest.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Only turtles reaching shore are counted; detection varies; dead/uninjured turtles are missed; species/sex/age may be biased.

solparts.label: e
solparts.html: Different habitats, surface-breathing behaviour, migration routes, body size or overlap with navigation channels.

solparts.label: f
solparts.html: Correlation and plausible mechanism support it; temporal trend is consistent; anomalous years and uncontrolled fishing/weather/reporting weaken inference; controlled spatial comparisons/tagging and more years are needed.

stem: Pathogens must cross body barriers before infecting tissues.

parts.label: a
parts.html: State two primary defences.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain why RNA viruses can evolve rapidly.

questions.title: Pathogens and defence

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Skin; mucous membranes/mucus and cilia; stomach acid; antimicrobial secretions. Any two.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Replication enzymes often lack proofreading, giving a high mutation rate; short generation times and large populations allow rapid selection.

stem: A myelinated neuron carries impulses to a skeletal muscle.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain saltatory conduction.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Compare simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain how a toxin blocking presynaptic Ca2+ channels affects transmission.

questions.title: Neural conduction and membrane transport

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Myelin insulates internodes; voltage-gated channels are concentrated at nodes; local currents rapidly depolarize the next node so action potentials regenerate node to node.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Both are passive and move down a gradient; simple diffusion crosses the bilayer, whereas facilitated diffusion uses selective channel/carrier proteins and can saturate.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Ca2+ entry falls; vesicle fusion/neurotransmitter release is reduced, so the postsynaptic membrane is less likely to depolarize.

stem: A root hair cell is transferred to a solution with a higher water potential than its cytoplasm.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain changes in solute and pressure potential.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain uptake of nitrate ions from dilute soil.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain why active ion uptake can increase water absorption.

questions.title: Water and mineral uptake by roots

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Water enters by osmosis; cell volume/turgor and pressure potential rise; solutes are diluted so solute potential becomes less negative until water potentials balance.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Proton pumps use ATP to create an electrochemical gradient; nitrate enters through co-transport/carrier proteins against its gradient.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Ion accumulation makes cell solute potential/water potential more negative; water then enters by osmosis.

stem: Ventilation maintains steep gas-concentration gradients at alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain inspiration caused by the diaphragm.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Name the muscles elevating the ribs during quiet inspiration.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain the role of surfactant.

questions.title: Human ventilation

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Contraction flattens the diaphragm, increasing thoracic volume and lowering pressure so air enters.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: External intercostal muscles.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Reduces surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse and reducing the work needed to inflate lungs.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

questions.title: Linked genes

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: AB and ab, the two most frequent classes.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: 10 map units/cM; linked genes are on the same chromosome and crossing over produces the less frequent recombinant classes.

stem: A gut community contains many bacterial taxa and changes after antibiotic treatment.
Answer 2 of the following questions. One additional construction mark is available for each response.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain what a short branch distance between two taxa on a cladogram indicates.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Define keystone species.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Distinguish succession from a climax community.

parts.label: d
parts.html: State how most bacteria reproduce.

questions.title: Community development and phylogeny

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: A recent common ancestor / close evolutionary relationship based on fewer sequence differences.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: A species with a disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to its abundance.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Succession is directional change in community composition over time; a climax community is a relatively stable late stage under prevailing conditions.

solparts.label: d
solparts.html: Asexually by binary fission.

stem: Carbohydrates have roles in transport, storage and energy transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain how monosaccharide structure relates to transport and polysaccharide storage.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain roles of the cytoskeleton in cells.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain the roles of NAD and NADP in metabolism.

questions.title: Carbohydrates and cellular work

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Monosaccharides are small/soluble for transport; glucose is readily respired; alpha-glucose forms starch/glycogen by condensation; polymers are insoluble and compact; branching allows rapid hydrolysis; beta-glucose forms strong cellulose fibres.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Microtubules form spindle fibres and tracks for vesicles; motor proteins move cargo; actin supports cell shape and movement/cytokinesis; cytoskeleton positions organelles.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Both carry hydrogen/electrons; NAD is reduced in respiration and donates electrons to oxidative phosphorylation; NADP is reduced in light reactions and provides reducing power in the Calvin cycle.

solution: Construction [1] Award for a coherent, logically ordered response using appropriate biological terminology.

stem: Specific binding allows signalling, catalysis and gas transport.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Explain receptor-ligand specificity in cell signalling.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain enzyme specificity and inhibition.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide by haemoglobin.

questions.title: Molecular complementarity

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: Ligands have complementary shape/chemistry to receptor sites; binding changes receptor conformation; signal transduction begins; only cells expressing the receptor respond.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Active site shape/chemistry is complementary; induced fit positions substrate; activation energy falls; competitive inhibitors occupy active sites; non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and alter conformation/Vmax.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: O2 binds reversibly to haem groups at high partial pressure and is released in tissues; cooperative binding gives a sigmoidal curve; CO2 is carried partly as carbaminohaemoglobin and mostly as hydrogencarbonate; H+ binding supports buffering/Bohr effect.

solution: Construction [1] Award for a coherent, logically ordered response using appropriate biological terminology.

stem: Evidence suggests RNA preceded DNA as hereditary material.

parts.label: a
parts.html: Describe RNA structure and evidence supporting an RNA world.

parts.label: b
parts.html: Explain PCR amplification.

parts.label: c
parts.html: Explain how mutation can alter phenotype.

questions.title: RNA, amplification and mutation

solparts.label: a
solparts.html: RNA is a nucleotide polymer with ribose, phosphate and A/U/C/G; usually single-stranded; base pairing allows folding; some RNA molecules are catalytic ribozymes; RNA can store information and catalyse reactions; core ribosome catalysis involves rRNA.

solparts.label: b
solparts.html: Heat separates DNA strands; cooling allows primers to anneal; thermostable polymerase extends from primers using nucleotides; cycles repeat; target DNA increases approximately exponentially.

solparts.label: c
solparts.html: Base substitution/insertion/deletion changes DNA; codons and amino acid sequence may change; protein structure/function may change; effects may be neutral, harmful or beneficial depending on location/context.
